newsitem.title: INDIA: India unlikely to sell Australian wheat to others.
newsitem.headline: India unlikely to sell Australian wheat to others.

text.p: India is likely to import a million tonnes of wheat it has contracted from Australia despite an anticipated bumper harvest and will probably not sell it to other nations, government officials said on Thursday.

"It is very likely that the wheat would be imported from Australia, but I don't think it would be sold to other countries," a senior Agriculture Ministry official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
India has contracted to import about 2.3 million tonnes of wheat from Australia, of which 1.3 million tonnes has already arrived. Another one million tonnes is due for arrival after July.
India has also bought some wheat from Argentina and Canada.
Indian Agriculture Minister Chaturanan Mishra said on Wednesday that India might sell the Australian wheat to other nations if domestic supplies and prices stayed under control.
But if traders hoarded grain, the government might use the wheat to control prices in the domestic market, he said.

The senior Agriculture Ministry official said on Thursday it was not easy to find buyers for a million tonnes of wheat. "Somebody has to be in the market. Finding a buyer for such a huge quantity is not an easy task," he said.

Mishra said on Wednesday that wheat output in 1996/97 (July-June) would be about 68.71 million tonnes, revised sharply higher from an earlier estimate of 64.66 million. India produced 62.62 million tonnes of wheat in 1995/96.
He said state agencies were expected to buy about 9.5 million tonnes of wheat for sale in 1997/98 (April-March) compared with 8.2 million last season.
The government buys wheat from farmers to build up buffer stocks and can then control prices by releasing grain through its distribution system.
Analysts said India might not import more wheat from Australia after an anticipated record harvest and expected state buying of 9.5 million tonnes.

"With procurement above nine million tonnes and expectations of a record crop, additional imports will not be necessary," said Shashank Bhide, a senior economist at the National Council of Applied Economic Research.
Reports from Australia said that the Australian Wheat Board had not held talks with India on the possibility that New Delhi might sell Australian wheat to other nations.

Industry officials said domestic supplies would increase by at least eight million tonnes in 1997/98 after an expected harvest of over six million tonnes. Two million tonnes of wheat has already been imported since December 1996.

"Hence no further imports of wheat are expected as the procurement, crop and stock position is expected to become quite comfortable," said Prem Garg, managing director of Shivnath Rai Harnarayan, a leading New Delhi foodgrains firm.
